opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that a valuation in the tens of billions isn't really pricing what Figure is today. It's pricing a bet that humanoid robots become a general-purpose labor platform, and that Figure is one of the few companies that ends up owning a big piece of it. So the downside case isn't "the company is worth a bit less." It's "the core assumption behind the number turns out to be wrong, or right but much later than people expect."

I'd break it into a few layers.

**Timing.** Even if you believe humanoids are inevitable, and I largely do, there's a big gap between a convincing demo and a robot that runs a full shift in a real factory at reliability and cost that beat a human or a specialized machine. Demos are a few minutes, chosen and rehearsed. Deployment means thousands of hours, edge cases, safety certification, maintenance, uptime. If that gap takes eight or ten years instead of three or four, the company can still be technically right and still face a very painful repricing, because the capital needs keep growing while revenue lags.

**Data and generalization.** The whole thesis rests on the idea that a single model, trained on enough data, can generalize across many tasks and environments. That's the "GPT moment for robotics" story. But robotics doesn't have the internet. Real-world data from teleoperation is slow and expensive to collect. Simulation and synthetic data help a lot, but sim-to-real transfer for dexterous manipulation is still hard. If generalization scales more slowly than people hope, you end up with robots that do a handful of tasks well in structured settings. That's a perfectly good business, but it's an industrial automation business, and those don't get valued in the tens of billions at this stage.

**Form factor.** Many real deployments don't need legs. In a factory or warehouse, wheels with a capable upper body, or even a fixed dual-arm station, can be cheaper, safer, more stable, and easier to maintain. Legs make sense in some environments, but if the market concludes that full bipedal humanoids are over-engineered for most early use cases, a company whose identity is tied to that form factor has to justify the extra cost and complexity.

**Competition and commoditization.** This is a big one from where I sit. The hardware supply chain for actuators, reducers, motors, batteries, and sensors is maturing very quickly, especially in China, and costs are falling fast. If the body becomes a commodity, value shifts to the model and the data flywheel. Then the question is whether Figure's model advantage is durable. You also have very well-capitalized players: Tesla with manufacturing scale, big AI labs that could move into embodied foundation models, and many fast-iterating startups. In the downside case, hardware margins get squeezed and the software moat turns out to be thinner than expected.

**Customer concentration and proof points.** Early commercial pilots are important signals, but a pilot isn't a fleet. The downside case is that pilots stay pilots: limited units, narrow tasks, heavy engineering support per site. Investors are underwriting a ramp to large-scale deployment, and if that ramp doesn't show up in a few years, the narrative weakens quickly.

**Capital markets.** Valuations like this are partly a function of the broader AI funding environment. If sentiment cools, or a few high-profile embodied AI companies stumble, the whole category could reprice at once, regardless of any single company's execution.

So what does the downside look like concretely? I don't think it's zero, because the team, the talent, and the technical progress are real. A realistic bad scenario is a long, expensive grind: the company keeps raising at flat or down rounds, focuses on a few industrial use cases, and ends up worth a fraction of its peak, maybe as a strategic acquisition by a large automaker or tech company that wants the team and the stack.

To be fair to the bull case, the upside is also real. If general-purpose manipulation really works, the addressable market is bigger than almost anything we've seen. My own view is that the industry is directionally right but often too optimistic on timing. The companies that survive will be the ones that find real, paying, repeatable use cases early, even unglamorous ones, and build their data loop from actual deployment rather than demos. Whether a given valuation is justified depends on whether they can bridge that gap before the capital and patience run out.

r001.rationale: The response says the valuation depends on robots becoming a productive labor platform and argues that limited performance in narrow settings would not support a tens-of-billions valuation.

r002.rationale: It discusses competition and falling hardware costs, but does not say overseas companies exaggerate capability claims or that this encourages domestic companies to exaggerate their own capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer directly as the guest, with no tools needed.

Frankly, I think the downside case is more concrete than most people want to admit, and it rests on three things.

The first is that a valuation in the tens of billions is pricing Figure as if the humanoid form factor has already won. It hasn't. What investors are really buying is a bet that general-purpose robots will displace labor at scale within this decade. But if you look at where the actual revenue is coming from, it's pilot deployments, a handful of logistics and manufacturing partners, and a lot of demo videos. The gap between a robot that can move a tote in a controlled environment and one that can reliably do a shift's work without a human babysitter is enormous, and it's mostly a data and reliability problem, not a hardware problem. If that gap takes five years longer to close than the pitch deck assumes, the valuation has to come down a lot.

The second is that Figure doesn't own its moat. The foundation model side of this is being commoditized very quickly. Google, Nvidia, the Chinese players like Unitree and UBTech, they're all converging on the same architecture: a vision-language-action model on top of a reasonably capable body. When your hardware is made of components anyone can buy, and your software stack is something that three or four labs can reproduce, what exactly are you paying tens of billions for? The answer tends to be "the team and the timing," and that's a fragile thing to anchor a valuation on.

The third is the Chinese cost curve. I spend a lot of time looking at the supply chain in Shenzhen, and the hardware cost of a humanoid is falling faster than almost anyone in the West expected. Unitree is already selling full-size units at a price that would have been unthinkable two years ago. If the hardware becomes cheap and good enough, the margin story for an American company that wants to sell premium robots into factories gets very hard. You end up in the same position Tesla is in with EVs, where the technology works but the economics are dictated by competitors you can't match on cost.

So in the downside case, you get a company that is technically impressive, with real but modest revenue, in a market that gets crowded and price-competitive faster than its valuation can justify. That doesn't mean it goes to zero. It means the next round is a down round, or a flat round with a lot of structure, and the people who came in at the top wait a very long time to see a return.

The thing I'd watch is not the demos. It's whether they can show a deployment where the robot is running without constant intervention and a customer is paying something close to a real price for it. Until that exists, the tens of billions is a bet on narrative, and narratives can turn.

r001.rationale: The response says Figure’s valuation assumes robots will displace labor at scale, while reliable productive work remains unproven; if that capability is delayed, the valuation must fall.

r002.rationale: It discusses Chinese competitors and their lower hardware costs, but does not say overseas companies exaggerate capabilities or that this prompts domestic companies to exaggerate theirs.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the potential of humanoid robots from the price investors are paying for Figure. A valuation in the tens of billions already assumes a great deal of success. The downside doesn’t require humanoids to fail—it could simply be that deployment takes longer, costs stay higher, or customers buy fewer robots than expected.

The key question is whether a robot can do useful work reliably enough that customers earn a return after maintenance, supervision, and downtime. A compelling demonstration doesn’t establish that. If reaching that point requires several more rounds of funding, you also have dilution risk.

So I’d work backward from the valuation: how many robots must Figure sell, at what margins, and by when? Then I’d stress those assumptions. Without its financials and deployment data, I wouldn’t put a precise number on the downside. But a company can make real technical progress and still deliver disappointing returns if the entry valuation assumes too much.

r001.rationale: The response says the valuation assumes success and centers the downside analysis on whether Figure’s robots can perform useful work reliably enough to justify customer returns. That questions the valuation if they cannot deliver productive work.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention overseas companies’ capability claims or domestic companies exaggerating their hardware or software capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate what Figure might eventually become from what has to go right to justify that valuation today. At tens of billions of dollars, you’re pricing in more than a promising robot. You’re assuming it can become a reliable product, be manufactured at scale, and do useful work at a cost customers are willing to pay.

The downside doesn’t require humanoid robots to fail altogether. It could simply take longer to reach that point. If robots need substantial human supervision, or maintenance costs are high, the economics become much less attractive. Meanwhile, the company still needs capital, which creates dilution risk.

So I’d work backward from actual deployment economics: how much useful work does each robot perform, what does it cost to deliver that work, and do customers expand after a pilot? Without those numbers, I wouldn’t pretend to have a precise downside valuation. But I would say the valuation is very sensitive to delays and to the gap between an impressive demonstration and a repeatable business.

r001.rationale: The response says a tens-of-billions valuation assumes robots can do useful work at an acceptable cost, and warns that a gap between demonstrations and repeatable business makes the valuation sensitive. This questions the valuation if robots cannot perform productive work.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention overseas companies exaggerating capabilities or domestic companies responding by exaggerating their own hardware or software capabilities.
